utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we begin today, Mr. Tieger, yesterday the accused filed his response to motion to admit testimony of Milan Tupajic in which he opposes the Prosecution motion filed on 16th of April, 2012. As the response raises challenges not covered in the motion including the applicability of Rule 92 quinquies to this case, in light of Rule 6 (D) of the Rules the Chamber wishes to know whether the Prosecution intends to file a reply to the response.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When can we expect to see that motion filed, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I was in the process of attempting to determine just that this morning. If I could give the Court a more accurate indication during the course of the day. Obviously, we understand, it's -- the Court would prefer this as soon as possible. That's our intention but I wanted to be realistic about that as well and so engage in some discussions aimed at making that determination as precisely as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'd like -- I would like that motion -- no reply to be filed no later than Thursday, tomorrow, COB.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. President. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic please continue. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, excuse me, Mr. President. I would like to address an issue with respect to the note verbale that was filed by France yesterday. If we could just go into private session for a moment to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we discuss it in the presence of this witness, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sure we can. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Could the Chamber move into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, yesterday -- or, actually, on Friday the government of France filed a confidential note verbale concerning our request to meet Milomir Stakic and pursuant to the Trial Chamber's public invitation, and I have two requests with respect to that. First, if you would order that it be reclassified as public because there is no reason whatsoever that the response should be filed confidentially and also if you would grant us leave to reply so that we could propose how to go forward from the impasse that appears to be reflected in the note verbale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As to the filing issue, whether in public or in confidentiality, the Chamber will take a look. So unless specifically indicated, so it seems prudent at the moment you -- if you file your reply confidentially as well, for the time being. Thank you. Could we move back to open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning, Excellencies. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you about an item. The description dating back to 1991, was it recognised -- did it recognise Yugoslavs as a special category? I'm talking about 1991 census.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I mentioned earlier, ethnicity was an open-ended question. That means any ethnicity could be reported by respondents, including Yugoslavs. There was no specific definition of who is a Yugoslav and who is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. However, in your analysis, you didn't single out Yugoslavs as a separate category. You mixed them with everybody else; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were part of the group called "others," together with ethnicities different than three major groups: Muslims, Serbs, and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that among those "others" Yugoslavs were so numerous that they account to a two-third to even three fourths of those others? Do you agree that it would have been more natural to add the others to the Yugoslavs rather than vice versa?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly how many Yugoslavs were there among others. Whether it was two-thirds or three-quarters, I don't know exactly. But the point of my analysis was to produce figures for three major ethnic groups, and for all remaining ethnic groups, there were also statistics to keep the analysis complete. But I had no particular interest in distinguishing from others, Yugoslavs and any other ethnicity reported there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your experience, who are those Yugoslavs? What is their origin?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, for me, they are Yugoslavs, exactly as reported in the census. But, of course, depending who is telling me who are the Yugoslavs, in some case, Yugoslavs will be Serbs, in some other case, Croat, in some other cases, Muslims. So, for me, they are Yugoslavs, as reported in the census.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. According to your experience, in 1991 when Yugoslavia was breaking up, how many Serbs were among Yugoslavs, and how many Croats, and how many Muslims?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Yugoslavs, for me, are Yugoslavs. So it is, you know, how people perceive themselves to be. They wanted to report them as Yugoslavs. Many of them were persons from mixed marriages. Many of them were people living in urban populations. They just didn't see them as one or another ethnic group. They wanted to report Yugoslavs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: With all due respect to your personality and your work, if you hailed from Armis [phoen] you would say that this was Communist propaganda. We have to look at the essence not the form. The form is that those were people who were in favour of the preservation of Yugoslavia by sacrificing their own ethnicity. However, did you notice that that category was very volatile? From one census to the next, their numbers changed. It did not have the usual dynamics in birth rate and mortality rate as the other three peoples?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is often forgotten, and you forget it as well, Mr. Karadzic, is that Yugoslavs and other reports on ethnicity are very sensitive to the formulation of this census question about ethnicity, and to the instructions the interviewers received when questioning people about ethnicity. The thing is that until 1971 census this wasn't an open question. Interviewers were deciding for people how to record their ethnicity. It changed since 1971. Since that moment, people could report whatever they wanted. This, of course, had a very serious impact on the numbers produced about ethnic groups. I recently saw a study in a journal, scientific journal, in which changes in ethnicity, definition of ethnicity, in the census were discussed. So it was not possible in this particular study to analyse phenomena by ethnicity for the entire period after the Second World War, starting with the first census, I think it was in 1948, until, and including the census of 1991. It was only possible to study ethnicity for the latest censuses that consistently reported about ethnic groups and about Yugoslavs. So what I'm trying to say, the definition of the question on ethnicity in the census has a fundamental importance on the numbers produced later. So if you don't look at the definition, you neglect the definition, and you look at the numbers, then you analyse something that is not, in fact, in the data. You have to take into account the consistency of definition on ethnicity used throughout the censuses or any other source studied.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will be very honest, Dr. Tabeau, and very open. 230-something thousand people were Yugoslavs in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Of that number, in 1991, probably as many as 200.000 were Serbs and when you separate them and join them with the others who account for one third or one fourth of that figure, then the picture, the ethnic structure you are portraying is completely distorted; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it isn't right, of course. What is the reason that you consider people who reported themselves as Yugoslavs to be Serbs? That cannot be done. This is changing the responses in the census. This is -- there is no justification of it and it is not right. You may not do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. However, not even you can merge a category which is fully recognised by the census with the others. We all know only too well who was in favour of Yugoslavia in 1991. Why didn't you portray them separately? Instead of doing that, you joined them with a minority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now you become argumentative. I think you've exhausted this issue. Let us move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please look at chapter 2 and Table 2. Or, rather, chapter 2, bullet point 1 where it is referred to the percentage of Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina in the municipalities referred to in the indictment against Karadzic. 41 per cent in 1991 and 32.8 in 1992 were the percentages we discussed yesterday. Did you establish what were the factors that had an impact on that decrease?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I think it will be easier if we go to the document, P4994. E-court page 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. My answer to the question, whether I studied factors that had an impact on this decrease, the answer is no, I didn't. However, there is a study of displacement of ethnic groups in the same report. So the change in ethnic composition should be looked at, together with the results on displacement. If I may have one more comment, yesterday we ended the day with a question why it is 19.9 per cent decrease and not 20 per cent. I checked, and, of course, this is what I -- was it was. It is a rounding error. The 41 per cent in fact is 40.9552. So these kind of small differences that cannot not be seen when only one decimal place is shown are responsible for this kind of little things in the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And that was about 8 percental points or 19.something per cent. Did you establish the difference between the Muslims who remained living in those Serbian municipalities and those who left?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, yes. If we go to the section 2.2, there will be minimum numbers of displaced Muslims given. So in the second paragraph in this section, we see the number 161.047 persons. So the rest of the 1997 Muslim population remained in the territory. In order to see how large the rest was, we have to go to the annex, to Table 2 for Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: E-court page 42.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So to the -- we don't see it on the screen yet. I will wait. So if we can enlarge the first row, information for the Karadzic case area, in the third-last column we can find the number 161.047. These are the displaced Muslims. But the entire Muslim population identified in 1997 is 283.199. It's the number to the left from 161.000. So from this table, you can also see that the fraction of displaced people in 1997 in the Muslim population was 56.9 per cent; also given in the same table, in the second-last column. Almost 57 per cent. So the rest are those who stayed. That would be 43 per cent, approximately. That is how you can find these numbers in the report, but, obviously, the focus of the report is on displacement. Therefore, the figures of displaced are discussed explicitly. It is also useful to take a look at the presentation discussed previously. If we go to page 2 of the presentation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To Table 4 at the bottom of this page.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: It's the next page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Table 4. In the second column where the minimum number of IDPs and refugees is mentioned, there is for Muslims the number 161.047, just discussed, and next to it, we have statistics on displaced persons from other ethnic groups. So there is a total of 286.972 displaced persons. Muslim -- persons of Muslim ethnicity are by all means the largest group of the displaced persons. This, of course, doesn't mean that every Muslim moved out. There is a group who stayed as well. So if it would be helpful to the Trial Chamber, I could make the same table for those who stayed, to have both statistics at hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Doctor, could you repeat the number of -- the total number.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The total number of -- minimum number of displaced persons from the Karadzic case area is 286.972.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's not shown on this table.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is shown on this table. In the last row, in the last row, where the totals are given --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- it is shown in the second column at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I see now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. And, of course, these are minimum numbers as we obtained the numbers from a sample; a large sample, but a sample.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And this is a specifically selected area or part of Bosnia and Herzegovina and in that specific part you express the figures in percentages. Let's look at the second line which refers to Muslims. Is it true that in 1991, there were 481.109 Muslims; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular area of 27 municipalities, that's the number of Muslims reported, those born before 1980.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now let's look at the next three columns. 161.000 is a minimum number. The estimated number is 284.000. Could you not establish that for a fact without any estimates? How would you have arrived at 59 per cent? Wouldn't it not have been easier to take that figure from the list of refugees?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I'm not sure what is the question about. If you could perhaps rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why did you use estimates in the third and the fourth columns where it says 284.000, to the fifth column where it says 285.000? Did you have at your disposal the register of refugees? Why did you not use the specific documentation issued by the Muslim government about refugees?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: For -- for the reasons we discussed yesterday, that it is important to be able to produce an independent study that would corroborate -- corroborate results from other sources, but, of course, there were also practical reasons. The register of internally displaced persons and refugees, the one of UNHCR, together with the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, had an information that was limited, for instance, in regard to ethnicity of persons, which, for us, was a crucial thing. Secondly, the register that we had at our disposal reports the situation as of the year 2000 which is even later than what we studied based on the voters' registration. For these reasons, among others, we rather used the sources like the population census and the voters' register.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you believe that an estimate or a calculation, even though you did not analyse trend, is more precise than the data provided by government organs?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I analysed the sources that I analysed because I found them reliable and meaningful and possible to be used in the analysis as ours. By the way, I checked the size of the voters' register of 1996 that we discussed yesterday, so at some point, there was a hesitation whether the size was bigger of this register than the register of 1997. So in 1996 elections, there were 2.396.000 voters registered. So 2.4 million individuals. In 1997, it is many more. So participation rate estimated for 1996 is 82 per cent. For 1997, it is 88 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we please take a look at Table 2A entitled: "Democratic changes in some municipalities in the Karadzic area." My page is 35, but I probably mixed them up because I was add some remarks of my own. While we are still on this issue, are you aware that in our law there is a distinction between residence and domicile? In our translation, it is said residence, but I'm asking you whether you know there is a difference between those two categories. If you don't know what the difference is, I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in demography, we call it de facto and de jure populations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: For example, you know where Zvornik is and Rastocnica is a big Serbian village close to Zvornik but belongs to Kalesija municipality. Now the residence of that person is in Rastocnica while his domicile is in Zvornik. How did you register such persons?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then I must say that my understanding of de facto and de jure is a different thing. I am afraid I don't understand what domicile is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Domicile is a place of permanent residence, whereas, residence is where a person lives and exercise many of his or her rights. But basically a person belongs to Rastocnica and in spite of the fact that he has to exercise many of his rights in Zvornik, in actual fact?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: In statistics, we have, as I mentioned, de facto and de jure populations. Census in the former Yugoslavia, and including the 1991 census, was related to the de jure population. Households where interviews were -- at the places where they lived, head of household actually was asked to provide information about any members of this household. Those who didn't live at this particular location were reported by the household and included in the questionnaire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And once the war broke out, this person went back to his domicile and then registered for elections in another municipality. How do we solve a situation like that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are two issues in the -- in the -- related to the registration of voters. The place of registration to vote is one thing, and there is another item, another variable. It is the municipality they wanted to vote for. So, in principle, people were supposed to vote for the municipalities where they used to live in 1991. However, if somebody became a displaced person, the person could vote as well for another municipality, a municipality where, in the future, this person wanted to settle down. In my analysis, I didn't study the municipality they voted for because it is not something not needed for my analysis. We studied the place of registration, place of registration, the municipality of registration, where people registered to vote. So this is a different item and has nothing to do with the voters' rights, any other rights people exercise at that time in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Uh-huh. But do you believe that a person could register in one municipality and go to vote in another municipality? Wasn't a normal situation that people registered themselves and voted in one and the same municipality instead of sending their ballot papers by mail as people did, people who lived abroad?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe registration is a process that took place before the actual election, so I'm not interested in what was happening at the time of election, when the actual voting was taking place. I'm looking at the registration to vote. And there were strict rules established by OSCE for the purpose of registration and for the purpose to prevent fraud. As I'm saying, people actually had -- could register in the municipality where they lived and voting could be later in person or by absentee ballot. It really doesn't interest me. It is the place of registration that I study because it is an approximation of the place of residence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But that was impossible, Dr. Tabeau. It wasn't possible for a person to register, for example, in Brcko and then go to vote in Banja Luka. You could only vote in the place where you are registered. So if you're a refugee in Brcko and you wish to vote for Banja Luka, the only way to do that is to register in Banja Luka; is that correct, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, people could register, once again, wherever they lived, and they had to register to vote in order to be able to vote. They could register in Brcko to vote for Banja Luka. That is possible according to the OSCE rules. In order to vote for Banja Luka, a person either had to live there by the time of 1991 census and be listed on the census of the Banja Luka population, or, if it was a displaced person who didn't want to return to Banja Luka, the person could register to vote for another municipality. The municipality of future residence, in this case, the person had to prove that it was possible for this person to settle down in this future municipality of residence. All this is regulated in the election procedures that was established by the OSCE and then monitored in the course of elections. Actually, the regulations were less strict in 1996 elections. So in 1996 elections, the procedure was deficient and made it possible for people to register to vote for several municipalities. And -- that was a very well-known fact. And based on the experience from 1996 election, the OSCE improved the regulations in order to prevent exactly this case. But all this has nothing to do with the place of registration to vote in 1997 elections. People had to register first in order to vote, and what we used in our study is the place of registration to vote.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, Dr. Tabeau, let's clarify one thing. If you have a person registering in Brcko and wants to vote in Banja Luka, in which voters' register is this person registered? In Brcko or in Banja Luka, regardless of whether he sent his registration to Banja Luka or went there in person, which means that he doesn't exist in the Brcko voters' register because he doesn't want to vote in the municipality of Brcko?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, if this person lived in Brcko, as a displaced person, and went to the registration centre next to his house in Brcko, the person will be registered in Brcko. And this is all that matters, for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But it will not be registered in Brcko, but, rather, in Banja Luka. There's no mention of this person in Brcko. He is going to vote for Banja Luka, regardless of where he is registered. And this can be a source of serious confusions if you believe that this person was actually registered in Brcko. Maybe you had been given erroneous information.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would like to comment on this, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Doctor Tabeau, hold on a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We have been over this subject for about 20 minutes, and I don't understand -- it's unclear to me whether perhaps the accused is misunderstanding what has been stated, but Dr. Tabeau several times has indicated that the only thing that mattered to her in her study and the only fact she took into consideration was where the person registered and that's important because that shows that that person is in a different location in 1997 than they were in 1991. For whom they voted for or for which town they wanted to vote in is irrelevant to the study at all, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There seems to be confusion as to the place where -- used to be where the voter is to register. So, Doctor, I think -- that seems to be pointed out. Why don't we let her continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, my comment is that related to the operation, way of operation of OSCE. During the 1997 elections, OSCE was extremely well prepared this time to be able to check every eligible voter from the point of view where they lived in 1991 because they had a complete list of eligible voters in every registration office. So it was a huge material printed census where people were listed, eligible voters were listed, and it was possible to check from Brcko where the person lived in 1991. So if the person lived in 1991 in Banja Luka, the person was checked and registered as a voter from Banja Luka, that is, entitled to vote for Banja Luka or a future municipality of residence according to his choice. But the place of registration will be still Brcko. So, in my view, there is absolutely no confusion about the place of registration at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So one can vote in other place than the place he lives currently, only if he was registered in 1991 election.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So the previous --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the 1991 census.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. The precondition to vote and register to vote was the fact of being registered in the 1991 census. And the place of residence from the 1991 census was also part of the registration procedure. Place -- these were municipal elections. People were extremely motivated to participate because they were electing local parliament. The people who will be at power after the election will end. So if you used to live in a municipality in, like Banja Luka, and you had your house there, and you became a displaced person, you were obviously interested to return to your house. So disregarding where you ended after the war, likely if you were a Muslim from Banja Luka, you ended in a place in the Federation with your family or friends or in a collective centre for refugees and displaced persons. You could vote from there. You could register there where you lived without travelling on the bus, or whatever else, and vote for your own municipality, from the place you stayed at that time of elections. Travel was very complicated at that time. It was not safe for all displaced persons to travel back to their homes and register and vote there. So this procedure OSCE developed was based on the actual realities in the country at that period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's just clarify one thing. If we have a person from Banja Luka registered in Zenica and he voted for Banja Luka, how did you count this person as being residing in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if the person resided in Zenica and registered in Zenica, the person is taken as registered in Zenica. At -- really, we should forget about, you know, the municipalities they voted for because this wasn't studied and this is an issue that is a separate issue. It only confuses the matter. We should really keep in mind that we looked at the place of registration where they registered to vote.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But hundreds of thousands of voters who were registered in the US, Canada, European countries and voted for their respective municipalities, in which category did you put these people?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were out-of-country voters. They had the opportunity to vote in the countries where they were staying at the time of elections. There is a separate category developed for them by the OSCE and procedure that was used in the election. So disregarding where they were living at the time of 1991 census in Bosnia, they could register from abroad and actually several hundreds thousands of out-of-country voters registered in 1997 election.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And they registered in New York City or in Salt Lake City, for example, because there are many of them. However, they did not appear in person. And you never included them in the tables because one has to bear in mind the fact that the majority of those who left for the US and other parts of America were Muslims but we don't see them here.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are included in the tables as a joint category of internally displaced persons and refugees. I always used in the report IDPs and refugees jointly. Of course, the first category, internal displacement, is a much larger component than the out-of-country voters. In the Milosevic report, Slobodan Milosevic report, there are several tables where this figure, joint number of internally displaced and refugees, is broken down into separately internal displacement and refugees. Refugees are underrepresented though - that means out-of-country voters are underrepresented, though - in my statistics, because the participation rate was not as high as for people who lived at the time of elections in the region of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But for the elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina, particularly during the first two or three elections, we had numerous sacks of ballot papers that had arrived from abroad. But if you did not count those Muslims who were the majority, there were, of course, some Serbs and Croats, then we have lesser number of Muslims. utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So if we look at this table where it says that Kljuc had .1 per cent of Muslims in 1997 is incorrect; right? I was referring to the previous table that we looked at under chapter 6.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is correct because what is given in the Table 2A for Muslims, for 1997, takes only the RS part into account.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Back to page 24.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page. I think it's page 25 in chapter 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us look at how the Serbs and the Croats were registered in these municipalities.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I am not sure that everybody understands what is the per cent mentioned in Table 2A for 1997 .01 per cent. utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we go back to page 43 briefly. So could you explain to us how the per cent of .1 can be reached from table.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. So in the RS part of Kljuc, in total, 21 Muslims are reported for 1997.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of them, 19 are displaced, so are gone, moved out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So just 2 remain in the same territory. 2 divided by 21, that's the per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's 10 per cent.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How do you come to 0.1 per cent.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps it is a mistake in presentation here in this table. I will check this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Serbian municipality of Kljuc, or, rather, Kljuc Ribnik in Republika Srpska consists of exclusively Serbian villages, and Ribnik not even in 1991 were there a lot of Muslims there? Did you establish how many Muslims were there in that part that eventually was given to Republika Srpska after the Dayton Accords were signed?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all I could establish is in this report. So I can again refer to the same table, 2M, or 1M. This is the table for Muslims. First one, 1M, reporting on the ethnic composition, and the second one on displacement, so from which we can take the numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 25 to see what the situation with the Serbs was in these nine municipalities. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: For example, let's look at Bosanska Krupa, and let's see how many Serbs were there in 1997.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: So if we can go to page 38, this is Table 1S, for Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I apologise. And what about this table that we have just had on the screen? What does it say to us? Does this table say that in Bosanska Krupa, in 1995, Serbs were the 100 percent population; in 1997, they were 99.5 per cent?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm thinking now what exactly these percentages show.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We can see that number in e-court page 39. So here we see 99.5 per cent in -- in the row of RS part of Bosanska Krupa.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, I think it is -- well, this 100 per cent for 1991 -- 1995, I'm not sure, but I think was reported by the authorities, RS authorities, who compiled these figures. I don't remember this. I have to check this. So that would be 95 per cent. 100 per cent. And 99.5 is the per cent that is given from this report for the RS part of Bosanska Krupa, which can be found in Table 1S on the screen. It is number 3, row number 3. Bosanska Krupa has three components, two of them belong to the Federation, and the last one is Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, do you know that only the village of Hasani was left to Republika Srpska out of all of Bosanska Krupa and it is simply because the great Serbian author Branko Copic hails from there? utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to comment on what you said about what happened in these territories because I'm not familiar with this kind of events. utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So that means the whole population in that part was reduced to 20 per cent.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why 20 per cent?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: From 4500 to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. But this is a sample, 980. It is not that we can take 980 as a complete population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a sample we are discussing. And we can relate the statistics, sample statistics, to each other, and this is what I have done when producing this 99.5 per cent of Serbs on this territory, as seen from the perspective of voters' data.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I ask you something? Is it correct that you said, for example, this third one, Bosanska Krupa, Krupa Na Uni, the total population according to the census of 1991 is 4.000, et cetera, and there were 2.690 Serbs out of that total figure; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what it says in this table, for the 1991 census population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In 1997, you say that 975 per cent [as interpreted] of the population are Serbs so your finding is that the number of Serbs increased from 2690 to 975. Well, that certainty doesn't look like an increase to me.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that how it has to be. Because for 1991 we have a complete segment of the population, from the census. It is those born before 1980, all of them, as reported in the census. In 1997 we work with a sample with those voters who registered to vote. So there is a group who did not register to vote. It is the 12 per cent of the voters' population eligible to vote, did not register. So 980 overall population in 1997 is a sample of the 1991 population. 975 Serbs reported here is a sample of 2.690. It's a sample. But it's a big sample that can be used to estimate the fraction of Serbs in 1997 in this territory. And this fraction is 99.5 per cent compared with 60 per cent in 1991 census. So there is a significant increase in the fraction of Serbs in 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where did these Serbs live in 1997? Did you establish that they lived in Krupa or did they report from somewhere to vote in Krupa but none of them actually lived in Krupa?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is again the same issue of voting for and registering in. As I said previously, it is all registered in this territory reported here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, Dr. Tabeau, Serbs from the Serb Bosanska Krupa are simply no longer there anymore in 1995 and onwards. There are no three parts. All of Bosanska Krupa belonged to the Federation then. Now let us look at the table in chapter 6, C, Serbs. Let us go back to that. Let us see what this looks like. Petrovac. What is the situation in Bosanski Petrovac? Can you tell us, while we're still on this topic, what the situation was with regard to Bosanski Petrovac? Line 5. Municipality 5.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Page 25.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So I want to make a comment about the municipalities studied in this report. We used the list of municipalities as defined in the post-Dayton classification of municipalities in Bosnia. This classification scheme was obtained from the OSCE and it was the same one that was used in the 1997 elections. But this is a dynamic system, it is possible that certain municipalities were redefined in a later time. So what is in my tables in the report, municipalities report, is consistent with the OSCE classification scheme for municipalities at that time. Going back to the table on the screen, on Serbs and Bosanski Petrovac for 1995, there is a number of 14.550 reported by the Serb authorities, RS authorities. And the per cent of Serbs in the 1995 population based on RS sources is 99.7 per cent. And the number in the next column for 1997, 99 per cent, can be -- can be found in Table 1S, Bosanski Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Page 39.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please take a look -- please go ahead. Please do go ahead?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just wanted to take everybody to the 99 percent in this table, for Bosanski Petrovac, for the RS part of Petrovac. It's in the second-last column. Petrovac RS it given 99 per cent. So these two are quite consistent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So in Bosanski Petrovac in 1997, were there 99 per cent Serbs or were there not that many Serbs?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: So this is what we can read in Table 1S. In 1997, there were 99 per cent of Serbs in the sample, 1997 sample, used in the study for the RS part of Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's a village that's called Drinic. In 1991, there was a population of 261 and then in 1997, 205. So in Bosanski Petrovac itself, 99.1 of the Serb population is missing, right, in the area that came to belong to the Federation; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Where do you read that 99.1 of the person Serb population is missing? If you can please tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, this table that have on the screen now, Bosanski Petrovac, and then Bosanski Petrovac in the Federation. The part in the Federation, I mean. It has 23 Serbs out of those thousands. 11.000, whatever. There are 23 Serbs left. So that is minus 99.1 per cent. There aren't there [as interpreted]. Almost 100 per cent is the figure of those who are no longer there.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic refers to the row above the one for the Petrovac RS. There are, in this row, for all ethnicity, the sample in 1997 is 3.415, of which 23 were Serbs. A very small per cent indeed, 0.7 per cent, not even 1 per cent. And my answer is, yes, that that is how it was. So the population movements, what we see for Petrovac, is not unusual. The population movements were having the opposite direction for those who were living in the RS and were moving to the Federation, and those who were living in the Federation and moving to RS. So it is easily understood if we think of what happened. The Dayton line divided certain areas into two parts: One was in RS; and one was in the Federation. And people, in order to feel safe, were crossing the Dayton line and going to their own people. I think this picture will be seen for many more municipalities. And if we go to the presentation that we discussed earlier, to page 2 of this presentation --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please take a look at chapter 6, Table B for Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that, Dr. Tabeau, how can we use this study in this criminal case? Who are we to hold accountable for what happened? The civil war or one of the parties? Because if it's the civil war that stands accused, I will join you in that. But what is the case?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Not -- it's not for the witness to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the witness said that she did not deal with establishing responsibility. However, the OTP called her with good reason and included a vast number of tables and 11 studies. So I'm interested in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please look at this. 1995 in Banja Luka. There's 10.500 Croats out of a population of 29.000, which was the case in 1991, as far as the Croat population is concerned; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That is 6.8 per cent, whereas in 1997 it is 2.6 per cent. From Dayton until 1997, two-thirds of the Croats left from Banja Luka. Percentage-wise that was less than in the period from 1991 to 1995; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- I think that you are mixing up certain percentages. It is, first of all, I don't know how do you know that two-thirds of the Croats left from Banja Luka. And more certainly the 6.8 and 2.6 are different percentages that have nothing to do with those who left here presented in this table. So I think it would be really useful to be specific about what number you are discussing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The first column that involves the Croats. 14.8 per cent in 1991 and in 1995 they accounted for 6.8 per cent. That is to say, 10.000 in relation to 29.000. So one-third remained. In 1997, again, one-third had remained from the population that was there when Dayton was signed. We're speaking in relative terms.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you -- you can, indeed, compare 1991 number of Croats, 29.026, with 10.500, but this has nothing to do with 6.8 per cent which is a different measure of a different thing. So obviously the number of Croats in Banja Luka dropped, and considerably so. There is no doubt about it. This is what we see based on the RS sources. But the 6.8 per cent is a measure of ethnic composition. It is how many Croats were there among all ethnicities in Banja Luka in 1995. It is a different presentation from what we see in my report and should be read also in a different way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. But it is quite clear here that in the general population there were 14.8 per cent in 1991. And then in 1995 they were 6.8 per cent in the general population. And in 1997 they were 2.6 per cent in the general population; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Percentage-wise in relative terms, this decrease from 6.8 to 2.6 is that not greater than the one from 14.8 to 6.8?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it is a misreading of this table. For sure, this table is not meant as a summary of the trend of what happened between 1995 and 1997. This table addresses a different issue, the issue of what was happening between 1991 and the end of the war, 1995, and whether figures from sources reporting on this provide a similar or different picture compared with what was produced in -- in my report. It is relevant to see how many people moved out from these municipalities as of early 1993 and how many of them were reported at the end of the war in 1995 and how their ethnic composition changed already by 1995 as presented by the RS sources. So 1997 figures are not included here as an expression of the trend between 1995 and 1997. It is just a separate measurement, separate analysis, coming from a completely different source than the RS sources, yet the numbers produced are similar. There is some uncertainty about these numbers, of course, so we cannot compare them directly and tell that the trend was from 1995 to 1997, this changed like that. So I think the intention of this presentation was completely different. Moreover, the RS sources were not used by me and my colleagues to produce statistics on displacement. Here, they are included for illustrative purposes of what was happening as recorded by RS authorities during the war already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: However, Doctor, in answer to the question of Mr. Karadzic can you not see here from this table that ratio of Croat people in Banja Luka has been reduced in 1997 compared to the situation in 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, the answer could be yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. I can see that, but I still have some doubts about the 6.8 per cent because the measurement was very approximate. This is not a methodology that can be taken as a source to produce exact figures.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellency, I see that you're mindful of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But let me just ask this: Do we agree that 14.8 per cent compared to 6.8 per cent is less of a difference than if we compare 6.8 to 2.6. That means that in relative terms there is a larger decline in the shares of the Croats in the general population from 1995 to 1997 than from 1991 to 1995. That can be calculated easily. Say, 1.1 or 1.3, and here it's basically 1 to 3.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't comment on it because I don't fully follow what Mr. Karadzic is calculating. What is the 14.8 per cent, for instance?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That is the share of Croats in the general population in 1991. 6.8 is the share of the Croat population in the general population in 1995. And 2.6 is the share of the Croats in the general population in 1997. So I'm saying that the decline is less when we compare 14.8 to 6.8, rather than 6.8 to 2.6. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's right. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll take a break for half an hour and resume at 11.05.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can I please ask for addendum B3 to be shown, demographic changes of the population in the area relating to some of the municipalities comprised by this case. That's Table B3.1.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While waiting for the right table may I comment on the problem with Kljuc we discussed before the break. We were looking at a wrong table. If we go to the right table in the annex, which is Table 1M, for Kljuc, that we can find the right number which is 0.1 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Shall we see that table first? Could you give us the number. Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: It's page 31.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So if we go to RS part of Kljuc there was a population in 1997 of 4.250 of all ethnicities and only 4 Muslims, which give us the 0.1 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But can we agree there were only 365 of them in 1991, and can we also agree that this is a rural area that was abandoned by the Muslims? That was not part of the urban area; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't study the character of these areas, whether they were rural, urban and how the orientation changed. So I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But do we agree that the number of the Serbs was halved in the section of Kljuc that was given to the Serbs? The total was 8.200 minus 365, which means that in 1991 there were around 8.000-and-something Serbs; whereas, in -- can you please help us -- yes. 4.250 in 1997. Which means that the number of Serbs was also halved; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's a sample. Did she not say those are sample numbers for 1997, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think so, Your Excellency. Because this is an estimate of the overall population. They may have made their estimates based on a sample, but this estimate relates to the entire population.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 1997 figures is a sample. 1995 figures coming from the RS sources, I understand is not a sample.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. This row says "1997 sample population."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But correct me if I'm wrong, based on a sample you estimated the overall population of Serbs in Ribnik; is that correct? This is not a sample. The sample was used as a basis for estimating the overall population.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, any figure for 1997 comes from a sample. I have never estimated the overall population size in 1997 using the sample. I estimated ethnic composition from that sample and numbers of displaced persons and refugees as minimum numbers. It is a different type of number than overall number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Again, it's not clear. What is 4.250? Is that a sample or is that a figure that you reached based on a sample? And what was the size of the sample?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you can take me to the figure of 4.250, please. Where is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Kljuc Ribnik 1997. Of 8.142 in 1997, this figure dropped to 900 ... to 4.250. So how did you reach this figure? Second line: .12 Ribnik, Republika Srpska, the total population in 1997 of all ethnicities is 4.250, whereas, this figure itself does not represent a sample. This is something that you reached on the basis of the census.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I am looking at the right table, which is Table 2S, page 51 of my report --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please look at the screen. I'm referring to the one that is currently on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I think the confusion as Mr. Karadzic was talking about the Serbs. This is a Muslim table. If we want to talk about the Serbs, we need to go to the Serb table.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Still, that all ethnicities -- numbers in all ethnicities -- I'm sorry. Ethnicities. Represent sample numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How can a sample exceed 50 per cent? How is a sample selected? And what does it represent?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we discussed very -- in a great detail how the sample was created. That is how the sample was created. If you distribute the numbers of voters from this sample according to municipalities and ethnicity, and, of course, you -- first, matched those records with the population census, this is how these numbers, as those on the screen, were obtained. But it is a sample.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, please, what we see on the screen, Table 1M, we can see that there were 8.142 inhabitants in Ribnik in 1991 out of which number there were only 365 Muslims. In 1997, the total number dropped to 4.250 with 4 Muslims only. It doesn't matter that this relates to the Muslims. One can clearly see that the drop in the number of Serbs is more than 50 per cent; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this table is for -- for the Muslims. And 1997 data is a sample. So you can't compare the absolute numbers from 1991 with that of 1997. For Kljuc Ribnik, for 1991, it is 8.142, and you can compared this number with 4.250; overall size you are saying in 1997. This is not correct. This is not the overall size in 1997. It is a sample for 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The sample of those registered to vote; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those registered to vote and matched with the -- with their census records.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And how many Serbs were there in Ribnik in 1997?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: So then we have to move to the Table 1S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Page 39.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: E-court 40, probably.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then for Kljuc Ribnik, we can read the number of Serbs is 4.207 out of 4.250 in the sample, which is 99 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But in 1991, there was 7.686 Serbs. How many were there in 1997?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now look at Addendum B3, please. Table B3.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us look at the first table. Can we agree that in 1991 there were 28.558 Muslims and 29.026 Croats in Banja Luka; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And 106.000 Serbs. Now let's look to the 1995 column. We have 10.000 Muslims, 10.500 Croats, and 125.000 Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do we agree that the percentage of the participation of Muslims and Croats in the overall population is affected by two factors: Number one, the real decrease of Muslims and Croats by two-thirds as a result of their departure; and, secondly, a relatively increased number of Serbs by two -- 19.000; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not entirely, but in big lines. I think the ethnic composition is an effect of changes in every ethnic group specified in this table.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But 14.6 Muslims and 14.8 Croats in 1995 the percentages are 6.4 and 6.8, respectively. It was affected by two factors: The real drop in the number of Muslims and Croats and the real increase of the number of Serbs, and it all had an impact on relative numbers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I said, in big lines, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do we see, then, in the period 1997/1998, the percentage of Muslims and Croats dropped to 2.1 per cent and 2.6 per cent, respectively?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is what is given here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we are now going to draw certain conclusions, the first drop from 14.6 to 6.4 was caused by the war. Can we agree that the decrease from 6.4 to 2.1 was the result of the Dayton Agreements, according to which people had liberty to choose where to live?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On what grounds? I don't see it. She is a demographic statisticians. She draws conclusions based on numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Okay. I will put the question this way: How do you interpret the fact that between 1995 and 1997, it dropped by two thirds? What was cause -- the cause of that? If the first drop was caused by the civil war, what was the cause of the -- of the second drop? That is what the statistics is supposed to show us.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Objection. In his question he has got a statement that somehow suggests she said that the first cause was the civil war. She never said this. She has never spoken about causes at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me narrow it down. Do you agree that this peacetime drop may have resulted from people's decision to change in -- entity?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I -- I want to comment on something else. There is a slight difference in how the two sets of numbers were produced. First of all, sources were different. Methodology was different. Time-period on which the sources' reports were different. So -- and the population covered by 1997/1998 and 1995 is different. 1995 is the entire population supposedly, and 1997 is 18 plus. Anyway, how I read these number, I look and assess the pattern in the number, so I look at the entire distribution for all ethnic groups. In 1991, 1995, and 1997/1998. And I see a change in the pattern that indicates an increase in the share of Serbs and drops in the shares of Muslims and Croats. That is my reading. And it has nothing to do with causes and processes that led to these changes. I report on the change in the pattern and that's it. That is all I am saying. And this is how -- where my role ends here. To study causes of migration a totally completely different approach would be needed. I would have to have a separate survey, investigating causes of migration to those who moved versus those who didn't. So it is causes of migration is a very complex issue to study in -- in a research.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we please move two tables down and let's look at Krupa. Do you agree that the number of Yugoslavs and others in Krupa literally disappeared?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what is in the table. They are not reported in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you noticed that there is some consistency in the drop of the number of Serbs and the drop of the number of others in the Federation municipalities and, on the other hand, the increase of the number of Serbs and the others in Serbian municipalities in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is what I mentioned today already, this opposite direction of movement of people from Republika Srpska and the Federation, and I included figures to illustrate these movements in the presentation. On page 2, Table 3, there is -- there are numbers who are showing this opposite directions of movements in both parts, but we certainly can't see that from the table for Bosanska Krupa in the annex which is on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please take a look the entries for Bosanski Novi. There were 2.121 Yugoslavs which accounts for 5.1 per cent. In 1995, it dropped to 1.7, and then in 1997 it increased to 4.5 which indicates that the number of Yugoslavs in Bosanski Novi municipality is on the rise if compared with the figures for 1995; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I completely disagree. Well, in these tables the reporting of ethnicity is the same in 1999 census and 1997/1998 because it is the same definition that is used. 1995 I have no idea, in the slightest idea, who is a Serb, who is a Muslim, who is a Croat and who is a Yugoslav, because it isn't the definition that was used in the census. So because you mentioned today that whether I knew that a majority of Yugoslavs were Serbs, so I assume that it is possible that the RS authorities worked on the same assumption, and where there were shifts between ethnicities and Yugoslavs in particular, which can be clearly seen for Banja Luka, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Am I right in thinking that here in the 1995 in the column of percentages for Yugoslavs we see the percentage of 1.7, whereas the estimates for 1994 and 1995 are 4.5. It is estimated that there will be almost three times more Yugoslavs than before. Please do not think that I am attacking you. I'm just trying to establish whether the methodology was valid, and can it allow us to draw conclusions about the movement of the population. I suppose that the OTP will also try to establish responsibility for that. Is it true that in 1995, it was 1.7, and then in 1997 and 1998 it was 4.5?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: But you have been doing exactly what you shouldn't be doing. You are comparing things that are not directly comparable. And, as I said earlier today, it is the intention to show the pattern in the ethnic composition and the change in this pattern as estimated from different sources. So I think it is wrong to compare the percentages as such. It is correct to look at the pattern, how the pattern changed from 1991 in 1995 and in 1997. The closer percentage to compare would be 1991 and 1997/1998 because of the same definition of ethnicity used in both cases. Even though the census is an entire population not a segment, still the voters' sample can be a good approximation of the entire population in terms of ethnic composition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then in terms of that pattern, how do you interpret this number? Ratio rose from 1.7 to 4.5 as regard Yugoslav and others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I interpret there was a decline in the Yugoslavs from 5.1 per cent in 1991 to 4.5 per cent in 1997/1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So can one now say that it rose from 1.7 in 1995 to 4.5 in 1997 and 1998.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would be careful when saying this. Why? Because it was not certain and likely it is not the fact that the Yugoslavs were reported in exactly the same way in 1995 as in the other years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then one should be also careful in comparing between 1991 and 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Of course. Of course. What really matters in this table is the population who moved out by 1993 because it is a number even though this number as well will be subject to changes in the definition of ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue, Excellency?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then I don't understand what the purpose is of highlighting these two percentages after the war, 1.7 in 1995, and then 4.5 in the latter years if it doesn't show that the segment of Yugoslavs and others was recovering in Serbian municipalities and falling in Muslim municipalities. Here we can see that from 1.7 it grew to 4.5, almost reaching the percentage that was present in 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what can I say? I can say comparing the percentages is not good, is not correct, because there are differences in the methodology and sources, how the percentages were obtained. But for illustrative purposes of the movement of population in 1993 and a result of this movement in 1995, as reported by completely different sources from what we used in this study, it is useful to present these tables.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay. On day one we agreed that the sources were different. I thought that there was no comparison between them. And that, on the one hand, we had the 1991 census, and on the other, all sorts of approximations and voluntarily registration for votes, and that those two -- those two could not be compared. Those are apples and pears, apples and oranges, and then you said that they were comparable and now you're saying that they are comparable [as interpreted], that different sources do not allow for any comparisons to be drawn, although you included all that in your tables.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: So, Mr. Karadzic, what do you want me to say? They are there as an illustration of what others were saying about processes that were happening during the war. My position is that the statistics I produced are reliable source for assessing of the migration during the war and changes in the ethnic composition. So that is the position. If you want a number, then please go to my work and take a number from there because I know how this number was produced and this number is reliable. About sources like this ones, I wouldn't advise to use them as statistics expressing exactly of what happened, but they do illustrate that things were happening in the war. That's it. That is the only thing that I am saying about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You used, Dr. Tabeau, the 1997 voters' registration and you just stated the numbers you reached is a reliable one. And -- but at the same time you are saying that the 1997 census that statistics is not 100 percent reliable. So that may be the question of Mr. Karadzic. Do you follow my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So it is that -- let's summarise. That the 1997 voters' register is not a 100 percent reliable source, yet I used this source to produce statistics. This is how I understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, voters' register is not a perfect source. Ideally we would like to see the next population census for Bosnia and Herzegovina to work with it instead of the voters' register. This census is unavailable. Voters' registration, as a matter of fact, is not as good as a census but it is broadly acceptable, reliable for the type of analysis in this report, presented in this report, a far better source, by all means, than the RS sources for 1993 and 1995. There is no doubt about it. The -- the numbers in these tables that we have on the screen are extremely approximate. How they were collected, for sure there was no questionnaire involved. There were probably inspections in these territories and rough estimates of how many people lived there. For sure there were no lists of names. For sure ethnicity was taken from, I don't know where. Certainly these were not respondents telling the inspectors about their ethnicity. So compared with the RS sources, voters' register is incomparably better. That is what I'm saying. And what I am saying is knowing that the RS sources are so approximate it is not good idea to get attached to these numbers too much because these are very rough approximations. The RS sources are good enough to tell, Look, people were moving out from these territories during the war, because as of early 1993, large population groups were registered to move out, and especially these were non-Serbs who were moving out from these territories. This led to a change in the ethnic composition. Already by 1995 the RS authorities noted this change because this is what they put in these tables. But in order to have a reliable estimate of ethnic composition, I rather would take everybody to look at the results from the voters' register because the estimation method was far more reliable.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at the following page and let's see what the situation was in Kotor Varos, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do we agree, Dr. Tabeau, that the absolute number of Serbs in Kotor Varos remained more or less the same? We had 14.056 in 1991 and 1.400 [as interpreted] in 1995.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In 1995, by using the estimate method, it was established that there were 1800 Muslims and a thousand Croats. And that was 10.7 and 6 per cent, respectively, in 1995. And now let's see how that percentage continued to fall between 1995 and 1997. The number of Serbs did not change meanwhile. And a possible increase in the number of Serbs did not influence the increase in the percentage of Serbs. The possible increase in the percentage of Serbs was influenced exclusively by the population movements of Croats and Muslims; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I see is that the share of Serbs increased from 1991 in 1995 and 1997 and the shares of other ethnic groups dropped. So disregarding the fact that the number of Serbs remained more or less the same, the other groups left, which increased the share of Serbs in the population. And a similar picture will be seen in other municipalities in this annex. In some cases, the numbers of Serbs will be higher in absolute terms, but, again, I would every time look at the pattern, how the ethnic composition as a whole evolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now let's look at the percentage of Yugoslavs and others in Kotor Varos, a municipality that remained in Republika Srpska. The participation of Yugoslavs and others rose from 2.7 to 3.4 per cent; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's conclude then. And before that, can we go to the following page and look at Prijedor and that will allow me to draw some conclusions. Is it correct that we can see both factors here. Both of the decrease in the numbers of Muslims and Croats, as well as the increase in the number of Serbs from 47.000 to 61.000. In 1995 there were 3.600 Muslims in Prijedor and 500 Croats at the same time -- - oh, sorry, a thousand Croats. And that was 5.4 per cent in the general population or 1.5 per cent in the sample. In 1997, the participation of Croats was higher than in 1995 and the number of Muslims dropped. In other words, Croats, Yugoslavs, and others returned to Prijedor after the end of the war and Muslims left. Would -- would you agree?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my reading is different of this table. Prijedor is a mixed municipality in 1991. The shares of Muslims and Serbs are comparable, about 43 per cent. Others, Croats and Yugoslavs and others, play a much less significant role. If I look at 1995 and 1997/1998, I see that this is a municipality strongly dominated by the Serbs in terms of their share in the population. The Muslims that were a significant ethnic group before the war are not there anymore and it is consistently seen in the data for 1995 and 1997/1998. Moreover, if we look at 1993, for Muslim, the population that moved out is 42.000 out of 49. It's a very huge number. This is what I am reading from this table. And the same for Prijedor can be seen in the municipal data in the annexes of my report where the population that became displaced of Prijedor, Muslim population, is extremely large.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what about Yugoslavs? How many Yugoslavs were there in Prijedor; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I don't remember. But Yugoslavs and other ethnic groups reported in Annex A5 for Prijedor is 9.295. That's the number from the 1991 census.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Of which two-thirds were Yugoslavs, and one-third were others; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what you are saying. I can provide this share, these percentages, but I have to produce them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at the 1991 census. There were 6.371 Yugoslavs and 2.600 others, according to that census. And among the 6.371 there were 6.000 Serbs in 1991 which was a large majority of the total number of Serbs. 6.371 on the one hand, 2.600 on the other. 2:1 ratio and this is a full picture. And with all due respect, this is what we call a Communist propaganda. They wanted to represent as many Serbs as possible as Yugoslavs in order to distort the ethnic picture of the population.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Objection as to it being a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What table are we looking at, Mr. ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm reading from the census, from the 1991 census which makes a distinction between Yugoslavs and others. And in all of the municipalities you can see that there are two times more Yugoslavs than others. Two-thirds of what Dr. Tabeau had under the category of others were Yugoslavs. And if you are familiar with the political movements in 1991 you would see that they're all Serbs. We will see what the population movement was. Serbs and others returned to the Serbian municipalities, whereas their number fell in the federal municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please look at Sanski Most. Was there a fall in the number of Yugoslavs and others there from 4.2? We don't have anything for 1995, but we have 4.2 in 1991 and then 2.4 in 1997.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: So if we look at the Sanski Most table, these percentages indeed are there, 4.2 Yugoslavs and others. I would call this group is just others as in my report. The percentage is 4.2, and in 1997/1998, 2.4.
