And, again, I want to stress, I didn't separate Yugoslavs. I studied them jointly with all remaining ethnicities different from the three main ethnic groups and this is how this data is also here presented, and I -- I didn't study how many Yugoslavs proportionally are there in this joint category, but I don't think it is relevant for -- for -- for -- for our discussion here because what matters is, as a matter of fact, the -- the changes related to the three main ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It is our position that this is very relevant because among Yugoslavs there were a lot of Serbs and that changes in the Serbian community are not presented as they should be because Yugoslavs were estimated wrongly and merged with all the others who were a big minority. It would have been correct, Dr. Tabeau, if you said Yugoslavs and then joined others to them because the participation of the latter was smaller. Instead, you merged Yugoslavs with others, and that's how you eliminated a huge number of Serbs from your calculations.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I can assure you I did not eliminate the Serbs from my calculation. I just processed the data according to how respondents defined themselves in terms of ethnic affiliations. Yugoslavs are reported, exactly as I am saying, Yugoslavs, and this is how I treated them in the analysis disregarding what you think, were they the Yugoslavs. You were saying a majority were Serbs, but it is not what I read from the census records. Yugoslavs are Yugoslavs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Very well. But why didn't you represent them separately from others, because the 1991 census recognises them which you don't do? In addition to having unreliable sources in 1995 and 1997, sources of different orders, we compound things even more by merging Yugoslavs with others, and, thus, we make any conclusion processed even more difficult than it should be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I think we heard enough as to the issue and notion of Yugoslav and others. It's for you to make submission later on, based upon this table and evidence of Dr. Tabeau. Why don't we move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just one question for you, Mr. Karadzic. You -- several times you ask the witness as to the changes or causes of -- in the ratio of population between 1995, 1997. How are they relevant to your case, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellency, there was a period of peace during which there was no enforcement or coercion, and there were demographic changes which were much bigger in relative figures than during war time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My question is how it is relevant to your indictment, the changes between 1995 and 1997? Or, Mr. Robinson, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I think it is only relevant in the sense that this witness has used 1997 demographic figures. If she hadn't done that, it would not be relevant at all. But those figures necessarily include movements that took place after Dayton and other developments. I think that's the point of talking about that period between 1995 and 1997.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Robinson. Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now can we deal with comparisons. Let's compare those municipalities which belong to the Karadzic case area in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Let us look at Table 2B1. I apologise. Image B2.1.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: That's 102.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Next page, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's page 100; the previous page. Yeah. No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then it's the previous one probably.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Page 100.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, please help us understand these graphs pertaining to population movements. The first table on the left -- or, rather, that image speaks of the share of the Serbs in the population as well as of Muslims and Croats, right, in 1991 and 1997? So we have 1997 marked with these lines; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, as a whole, the number of Serbs in 1997 was mildly on the increase, also, the number of Muslims. Whereas, the number of Croats is slightly declining; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is ethnic composition but these are not absolute numbers. These are fractions, percentages, that are shown for the entire territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The next one is in the area that is called the Karadzic case area, 1997. There is a certain increase in the number of Serbs and a certain decline in the share of Muslims and a decline in the number of Croats; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If we look at these graphs, Dr. Tabeau, does this seem fairly similar to you?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please take a look at the one further down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the part of Bosnia-Herzegovina that belonged to Republika Srpska, we have a further increase - relative - in the number of Serbs and the number of Muslims was decreased by some 60 per cent, right -- sorry the number of Serbs compared to 1991 and 1995 and then compared to 1997, there's an increase in the number of Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And we also see the situation as far as the Croats are concerned. Can we have a look at the next one now. Now the numbers of the Serbs in the Karadzic case area, so that is less that Republika Srpska, as such. Do we agree that in the Karadzic case area that belonged to Republika Srpska the number of Muslims -- or, rather, the share of Muslims is somewhat greater. Can you please explain this to us?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: What can I explain? These are two areas. One is the entire country and Karadzic case area are 27 municipalities. For these two areas, the same type of statistics were compiled and are shown here on these charts. There are slight differences, indeed, in the number -- in the share of Muslims in Republika Srpska compared with the entire Bosnia and Herzegovina. So the share of Muslims in the Karadzic case area is very slightly higher than in the entire Bosnia, which is absolutely possible, because this is ethnic composition percentages, so it's possible. I wouldn't say that the difference is really very significant here. What is striking in case of Republika Srpska is that the share of Serbs increased very significantly in both areas, in the entire Bosnia and Herzegovina -- in the RS part of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the RS part of Karadzic case area. And the opposite is seen, the lower charts showing the Federation part of Bosnia and Federation part of Karadzic case area, then we see that the share of Serbs declined and the share of Muslims increased.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now you're talking about the last one on the right; right? So what was under Serb control. The Karadzic case area, that is. Once it came under the control of the Federation after Dayton, the share of Muslims in that area is over 80 per cent and that is more than in 1991; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: On next page, there are numbers -- well, percentages shown. So for Muslims in 1997 in the FBiH part of Karadzic case area, we see 86.4 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do we agree then that in peacetime, in the territory that was under Serb control, changes occurred, demographic changes in the following way: Serbs practically disappeared from areas that they had controlled up until Dayton; and the number of Muslims rose to 80 per cent, so there was exchange of population in peacetime. There was an exchange of population or population movements in peacetime. Can we go back to the previous page. They're practically no Serbs in the territory that used to be under their control. But am I right if I say that? Am I right if I say there are no Serbs left, although they had had it under their control? But, ultimately, it came to belong to the Federation and then there were no Serbs left, whereas there are more Muslims than there were in 1991?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. First of all, you said changes were happening after the Dayton Agreement was signed in the peacetime. So I can't agree with this because we already had a very long discussions this morning about changes that were happening in the course of the war. In 1993 already large numbers of the population moved out from municipalities in the Karadzic case area. But, indeed, what we see in these charts is -- is a summary of how the changes were happening. So from RS part, non-Serbs were moving out, and from the FBiH part, the Serbs were moving out. That is what summarised in Figure B2.1 and we see it very clearly for both, for RS and FBiH areas of Bosnia and Herzegovina and for RS and FBiH part of the Karadzic case area. That is the picture that is obtained from voters' register but similar charts were produced by other organisations, including the UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, let us now focus on the second and sixth graph. In the second one, the entire Karadzic case area is included, in the Federation and Republika Srpska. And we see there an increase, not that sharp an increase in the number of Serbs and not that sharp a decrease in the number of Muslims. So that would be the area that was under Serb control. However, not all of it came to belong to them. Now the area that was under Serb control and that came to belong to the Federation, that is graph 6, we see a drastic decline in the number of Serbs, a significant increase in the number of Croats, and a drop in the number of Croats, and so on. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, how much time will I have? That is what I'd like to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How much do you need, Mr. Karadzic, more?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I believe that I'm not even close. I have all of today, don't I? That's the amount of time that you had allocated to me, or perhaps there's 15 or 20 minutes left. Could Ram help, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was of the impression you may not need all of that. But, so far you have used four hours and 40 minute, which means you have this session and some time -- an hour in the next session. Probably you can finish by the end of today. It's better to conclude Dr. Tabeau's evidence, including re-examination, by today. But we'll see.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'll do my best. Thank you. Could we now please take a look at 2A that has to do with Srebrenica. It's page 80 in my papers. But perhaps we should just take a look at 2A, the results for Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Is Mr. Karadzic talking about Srebrenica internally displaced people or the Srebrenica report because I don't think we know what report we're talking about here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Results for Srebrenica: Share of the Muslims in the population of Srebrenica. And then after that is Table 2A.1.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Page 68.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please move onto the next page for a moment, page 69.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Am I right if I say that towards the top where it says Table A2.2, you say that there's a distinction between an internally displaced persons who lived elsewhere in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1997 and refugees, persons who lived abroad in 1997? Did you apply the same criterion into those 27 municipalities, or nine municipalities, and all of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or is it believed that only the people of Srebrenica lived abroad?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all municipalities were subject to the same methodology. But for Srebrenica, here in this annex, more detailed results are also included.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But this is what I'm interested in: For those 27, or those nine municipalities, or for all municipalities for that matter, in all of Bosnia-Herzegovina, did you establish the number of persons who were abroad?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same analysis was completed for all municipalities as well, for the entire Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then I must have been inattentive because in other municipalities, I did not see that you singled them out in this way, saying who lived abroad. If you help me, I will be glad to accept that.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we didn't present separate figures on internal displacement and external displacement, that is the refugees for all municipalities, in the same way as for Srebrenica. It is just an sample. Srebrenica is an example included in Annex A2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, that is exactly what I asked about. What about the other municipalities, as far as that segment is concerned? The same methodology was not used for all municipalities, right, or not all results were shown according to the same methodology?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The results shown in the report is a selection of major figures. If the need will be, then if you are interested in refugees, also these figures can be produced separately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But for Srebrenica, we can get the number of refugees aboard and we cannot do that for other municipalities; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not right now, but in Slobodan Milosevic report there is a selection of more municipalities presented in exactly same way as Srebrenica, yes. Well, I -- I don't think it is really crucial to make this distinction between internal displacement and refugees, but if needed and essential, these figures can be additionally provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well. Now that we're op this page -- actually, it would be better to go back to the first page, if possible, please. Please let us take a look at Table A2.1. In 1991, in Srebrenica, there was a population of over 29.000; isn't that right? And 21.300-something were Muslims --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot keep up with figures that are being read at this pace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot catch up with your speed if you read that fast. Could you repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, we see the numbers here, don't we? The total population in 1991 was 29.198, as established in the census. Out of that figure, two-thirds were Muslims; one-third were Serbs; and almost 600 others; whereas, Croats accounted for 35 persons. Now applying the methods -- or, rather, the information that you had collected by different sources for different purposes, isn't that right, the total number of inhabitants in 1997 was estimated at 7.422; 7 Muslims, 7.169 Serbs. Do we agree that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, where did you get that idea of total number of inhabitants in 1997 having followed Dr. Tabeau's evidence so far? Dr. Tabeau?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a sample of those registered in 1997 in the municipality of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, Your Excellency, here in the first column, line 2, it says: All. And then it says 7.442. That cannot be a sample. That can only be the total population. If this is just a sample, what would be the total number of inhabitants?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may say, the "all" refers to all ethnic groups. That is the indication who is reported, "all ethnicities" jointly. But, of course, the 1997 numbers are obtained from the voters' register. That means it is a sample, not the size of the population in 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, if 7.442 is the -- a sample, what is the total number of inhabitants in 1997?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said today, I don't know. I don't have this number. I don't have the overall size of the population in 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How then, if we look at column 1, line 1, how can that be linked up to column 2? What is the point of placing these numbers one next to the other?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The point is that we can calculate - and rightly so - percentages. That means we can obtain the ethnic makeup for 1991 and, as well, for 1997. For this, we work for 1997 with a sample data and the percentages calculated are in the second part of the same table. Percentages can be compared between 1991 and 1997. That is justified and correct. Not the absolute numbers though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How shall we read the third and the last row? 1991, 1997 change.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That this is relative difference that we discussed yesterday. So 73.2 is the per cent of Muslims in 1991 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, the last one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I'm going to. And in 1997, the percent of Muslims is 0.1. So the difference between the two, 01 minus 73.2, divided by 73.2, makes 99.9 with a minus. Is the change in the share of Muslims between 1997 and 1991, expressed in relative terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How shall we read the next number: Plus 290.4.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is 96.3 per cent of Serbs, minus 24.7 per cent, divided by 24.7 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And there are three times more Croats; right? Plus 281.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is what it says here. Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, let us go back to the first two lines. Are these absolute numbers?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these are absolute numbers, for 1991 and 1997 in the second row.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that in 1997, there were about 50 less Serbs than in 1991?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hmm. We just discussed that 1997 is a sample and 1991 is the overall size of the population. So what we can do we can think of comparing 7.169 with all ethnicities number, which is 7.442 which give us 96.3 per cent of Serbs in 1997 population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I don't know, Dr. Tabeau, how you can say that these are absolute numbers. How did you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I think, Mr. Robinson, now, I take it you understood Dr. Tabeau's point. All the number, absolute numbers in relation to 1997 are related to voters' register. I don't think Mr. Karadzic has understood that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm sure he understands that, that that's the only number that -- otherwise any discussion of the report is meaningless because that's the only number she used to compare the 1991 results. So even though we all understand that that is a sample or it's not just precise as the census, it's the basis of the discussion of her report. So I think he understands that very clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He may continue this same question with respect to every table. Shall we take the break now and then ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That would be fine. I just wanted to take a look at the table for a minute, the next one, but if you wish, we can do it after the break. Table A2.2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It has to do with 1997 voters originating from Srebrenica, right? And then in Srebrenica, there are -- actually, they're there in 1997. Can you explain this to us, 3.237. These are voters who are still in Srebrenica; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the voters who were still in Srebrenica in 1997. Well, this table is a different type of statistics than what we discussed previously. In order to define population movements and decide who moved, who didn't, it is necessary to trace in the voters' register the entire population who originally lived in a given municipality. It's, in this case, Srebrenica. So in the voters' register, there was a total of 13.891 voters who used, in 1991, to live in Srebrenica. That's the total, 13.891.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 10.654 out of that number voted for Srebrenica, outside Srebrenica; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know and don't want do know how they voted for which municipality. I only know that 10.654 registered to vote in a different area than the Srebrenica municipality, where they used to live in 1991. And only 3.237 of the original 1991 population of Srebrenica municipality registered in Srebrenica. As we see, almost all of them were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Dr. Tabeau. How does this number square with the previous number we saw in the previous page, if you remember, the number of 7.442?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was waiting for this question. It's a different population. It's a different population in the sense that voters who registered in certain places can be regrouped in various ways. In the previous table, we have the number of all those who were identified themselves, registered themselves, in Srebrenica. All of them. Not originally living in Srebrenica, all of them. There are newcomers in Srebrenica. So one group of population goes, and another one comes. So if we count all of them in Srebrenica in 1997, then we have the number, 7.442. This number comprises the number of 3.237 from Table A2.2. But the 13.000 is a different population. Different in the sense that voters here are regrouped according to the place of residence in 1991, which obviously, for a large number of them, was different in 1997. This is 10.654. So these two perspectives are there in the report, and it is not a mistake that in Table 2.2, we have the 13.000 related to Srebrenica, and a different number in Table 2.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a second --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can take the break now, Excellency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can take the break now, and then we can pursue this topic after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I would like you to organise your -- the remainder of your cross-examination to be concluded in an hour's time in the next session. We'll resume at 1.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.33 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would just briefly deal with Srebrenica and then we will move to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us look at Table A2.2. According to that table, there is an estimate which shouldn't be an estimate but, rather, an established fact that 9.726 Muslims registered to vote in the 1991 elections; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there is a number of 9.730 Muslims have been identified, who, initially lived in 1991 in Srebrenica municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But they were registered to vote in the 1997 elections. Look at the title of the table under A2.2.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I just said. 9.730 Muslims from originally Srebrenica municipality registered to vote in 1997 elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. They registered where?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Four of them, in Srebrenica; and 9.726 at other locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In other words, they were not represented in those places where they registered; but, rather, in that place or those places where they wanted to vote and where they voted.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what is the question. I just confirm that 9.730 from Srebrenica municipality who used to live in Srebrenica municipality, according to 1991 census, this group of Muslims from Srebrenica registered partly in Srebrenica, only four of them, and the rest of them, 9.726, at other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: For voting in Srebrenica; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't check what -- for what municipality they voted. I am not interested. I am interested in where they registered to vote: Four of them in Srebrenica; 9.726 not in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But they were registered elsewhere; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Elsewhere means not in the Srebrenica municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does it also comprises [as interpreted] the so-called third countries, either in Europe or overseas, in America?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We can move to Table A2.3, on page 71. So in the first table A2.3a, we see for Muslims the overall total, 9.730 in the last column. Of this number four were located in the Srebrenica municipality and therefore are considered to be not displaced. The rest is falling under two categories. There is 8.002 of IDPs, that is internally displaced persons, and that 1.724 in the next column are the refugees from Srebrenica in third countries other than Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And of that number in Serbia, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in Montenegro, in Europe, and in America, you think that only that many were refugees or only that many registered to vote?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is the registered voters, of course, and it is a sample, not the complete population of refugees in third countries from Srebrenica. So it's a small group, very small group. And most of them were outside the region of the former Yugoslavia, as shown in Table A2.3c the last table on this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you perhaps notice that the participation of Serbs in percentages among the displaced, those who died, and so on and so forth, equals to the participation of Serbs in the overall population, and that in Muslims, that number is somewhat higher on account of the fact that it is somewhat smaller among Croats?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think you are taking here a shortcut, speaking of those who died. So far, we haven't discussed any deaths at all. So I don't really know what are you referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm actually implying all the suffering, including displacement and other things. Did you notice, did you try to find out how many Serbs suffered through the war, and what was their representation in that number with regard to the representation of the Serbs in the overall population?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are referring to rates of suffering, as you call it, by ethnic group, all I can offer you is this report, which, actually, doesn't contain any rates, just numbers, minimum numbers and certain percentages describing this number, the estimated number, in relative terms. I have made a number of other reports on victims in all these reports. I tried to quantify numbers of victims, again, in most cases, this would be minimum numbers for all ethnic groups, including the Serbs. I think that is all I can offer you, but you wouldn't like to engage in a discussion that would lead to comparing the suffering of ethnic groups among themselves. I don't think -- I wouldn't like to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Can we now look at Table 1.BH. This is the percentage of the population, and we're talking somewhere on page 70.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I think this is 66.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So the percentage of given ethnic groups in the population of Bosnia and Herzegovina status as of 1991 and 1997. Help us understand this. We're looking at the population as it was in 1991 and then what you call the sample and, in my view, this is a percentage that was obtained based on the sample as it was in 1997. Do we agree, can we agree that there were three and a half million adults and there were about 1.150.000 Serbs?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I have the page number? Because I can't see on the screen all the numbers. Then I can find it in my report.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Page 65.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you were saying there were 2.565.000, approximately, all ethnicities population in 1991, of which 1.147.900, so 148.000 almost, were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Those are all the people who were born before the year 1980; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What is the meaning of the next absolute figure of 1.800.000 of all ethnicities? That would be a sample of the total population of Bosnia and Herzegovina, about one-half of the actual total population; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the voters' records from 1997 elections that were used in the analysis for Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is all ethnicities; 1.800.000. 1.8 million.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What would be the total participation in that? How did you arrive at the figure that there were 3 per cent more Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina? You say that the participation of Serbs rose by 3.1 per cent in Bosnia-Herzegovina; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be helpful if you would tell me exactly where I am saying this. I -- I can't -- I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Line 1 is about the share of Serbs in the overall population in 1991 and the sample in 1997. And you say that the number of Serbs rose by 3.1 percentile points, or 9.7 per cents?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I can see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How did you arrive at that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought we discussed the methodology at length earlier during my testimony, at several occasions. So I don't think I really need to repeat all this again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Doctor, to understand the context, where did 0.7 million go? Because I remember the total number of registered in 1997 was 2.5 million.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. But here we are talking about the matched records exclusively, so this number, 2 and a half million is, of course, lower.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And the percentage, the 32.2, from the census, and the 35.3, are just the shares of the Serb population in both years. So what more can I say about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But look at Muslims. We have 42.2 per cent and then we have an increase to 45.5 per cent accounting for 2.3 percentage points, and in your analysis, that was 7.7 per cent more. And all that at the expense of Croats whose percentage or share fell from 17.7 to 13.4 per cent. And the others, the other ethnicities also lost in numbers.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still don't know what -- what is the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to see how can this table be of benefit when we are looking at the movement the population. Do you know what part of the territory in Bosnia and Herzegovina was controlled by the Serbian side during the war? Do you know that the surface of that territory accounted for more than 70 per cent of the total territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina at times?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, this is your claim. I -- I didn't produce these kind of numbers in these reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now look at the third table in here, 3BH. Help us, please, to understand. Is this an estimate, according to which all there were about -- or exactly 1.306.000 displaced persons and refugees and that 406.000 to 410.000 of them were Serbs?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the correct reading of this table.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm going to tell you that in the DP population that was 31.4 per cent, whereas there was 32 per cent of the Serbs in the overall population. I wanted to ask you that. I made my calculation and I'm asking you whether you noticed that the share of Serbs among the displaced persons and refugees more or less corresponds in the -- to the share of Serbs in the overall population. Did you notice that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it might. I -- I -- and -- what -- what does it mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, I'm -- again, I'm not attacking you. I am on trial here because the Serbian side allegedly prosecuted [as interpreted] all the others, and I want to see the entire picture. Let's look at the Muslims. Among the same number of displaced persons, there are 42.4 per cent of Muslims, whereas the share of Muslims in the overall population was 44 per cent; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, it might be so. And I don't feel attacked, Mr. Karadzic. I don't take your questions as being attacked. I try to answer your questions, but who said that the losses, or displacement in this case, of each ethnic group have to be proportional to the size of this group. It might be proportional or not, depending on what happened. The purpose of my report this -- on municipalities is to provide numbers of displaced persons, in terms of both minimum numbers and estimated, overall numbers, and that is what we see, estimate, in the Table 3BH, for the entire country. And that is all what I'm saying. I have the numbers and whether they are proportional or not is a different thing here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Tabeau, you are testifying in a criminal matter concerned with establishing my guilt. Are you -- you were right -- you would be right if you were working on behalf of a government. But I have to drive them -- the matter home and I am trying to show to you that the shares of Muslims, Croats, and Serbs in the overall population are the same as their shares in the -- in the population of displaced persons. Let's look at the Croats. Their number is about 1.300.000. Actually, the overall population is 1.300.000, and there are about 18 per cent Croats. And you will remember that the participation or share of Croats in the overall population was also 18 per cent?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: And? If it was?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It is my thesis, Dr. Tabeau, that what happened over there was a civil war. It was not that the Serbs persecuted others and nothing happened to the Serbs and everything happened to the others. You will realise that everything is proportionate here. There is always a good proportion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think Dr. Tabeau has given her answer already and how to interpret and how to make your submission it is for you to do later on and it is ultimately for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Excellency. Thank you. However, you would be right in saying later perhaps or asking me why I did not present my -- that interpretation of figures for Dr. Tabeau, and this is what I am doing, in order to prevent that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I intervened because you asked for the causes of this displacement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now, let's move onto Sarajevo. You mentioned several things that concern the criminal, legal qualification or perhaps political qualification, and so on and so forth, and let me ask you this: Did you establish that Sarajevo was under siege? Did you do it yourself or did you take over that qualification from others?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't establish or I didn't work with the qualification that Sarajevo was under siege. I just used a survey conducted by others to produce numbers of victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you said that Sarajevo was under siege. Are you saying that Sarajevo was under siege or will you agree with me that Sarajevo was a city divided, not Leningrad, but, rather, a Beirut?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would suggest to go to footnote 1 in the first Sarajevo report, Karadzic report, which the term "siege" is used to refer to events in Sarajevo as they become popularly known.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I must fight what people see as a notorious facts. Let's move on. Did you mention the fact that victims in Sarajevo were victims of terror?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was one of the conclusions that, most likely, yes, there was a terror campaign against, in particular, civilian victims in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This calls for a bit of analysis. You said that you arrived at that conclusion when you applied a formula on the proportion of civilian casualties on the one hand and military casualties on the other; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These two were compared.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This proportion, or, rather, this formula, is it the same when it comes to international conflicts and when it comes to internal conflicts or civil wars?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know why would be this relevant, what kind of conclusions can be drawn from this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm kindly asking you to tell me just this: Is this a single formula and a single proportion that is equally applicable to international conflicts as well? Yes or no. Both to international conflicts and civil wars, is it equally applicable?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that it is a part of the law of war, that civilians need to be protected in any conflict. So equally, as well in the international conflict or internal civil war, civilians are a protected group of the population during any armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We're not disputing that. What I'm interested in is: When you draw a conclusion that more civilians were killed than collateral damage as such would be permissible, did you have in mind international conflicts as well, and did you think that the same criterion applies to them, or no?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't discuss the collateral damage explicitly as such in my reports. I did a sample analysis in which I compared the number of killed civilians with the number of killed soldiers. As exactly the same thing is with the collateral damage, there is no prescription, no exact number that could be used as a reference standard in any court proceedings to tell what is the cut-off point beyond which we -- we don't speak anymore about the collateral damage. The same refers to the work I provided on Sarajevo, so there are no prescriptions and reference standards, but the common understanding tells us if the number of killed civilians are much higher than those of killed soldiers and for -- on many days during the combat activities, then something is wrong with this fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did I misunderstand, that there exists some kind of coefficient which indicates whether those were accidental civilian victims or intentional victims? Is there any way to establish exactly the ratio between the killed and wounded civilians and killed and wounded soldiers. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said there exist no reference standard as such to be used in analysis like the one I -- I completed. And in court proceedings, it is a term, collateral damage, or, you know, disproportional killings, civilians in relation to soldiers. It is a phenomenon that needs to be carefully studied and decided upon what is in the results of an analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that the coefficient that you applied when you were deciding when the number of victims was excessive, was it something that you, yourself, created or did you adopt it from somewhere else? But, first of all, refresh our memory. Did you say that a coefficient is to be applied and that if it is less than one or more than one it means something; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I did -- I didn't create a coefficient. I studied two variables: One was killing of civilians observed day by day and the same with killings of soldiers. It was just a comparison of the two I completed in order to draw certain conclusions. This kind of comparisons are often made also in other conflicts but it doesn't mean that we have a coefficient here. It is a simple comparison of two types of killings: One of civilians, one of soldiers, and that has been done much more frequently than just me. Second, what I said, that there is no threshold for collateral damage or for the number of killed civilians per one soldier. That is all I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But did you explain to us the coefficient that is using Index 1?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is not a coefficient. It just if you divide one by another, then the value might be one, might be lower than one, or higher by one. That's all I am saying. If it is one, then the number of civilians is exactly the same as the number of killed soldiers, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And who set this standard?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is how it is. If you divide two by two, the number is one. Exactly the same if you add two plus two, the result is four. There is no rule, no regulation, no coefficient. This is how it is. You divide one number by another. If they are the same, the result is one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. And then in certain armed conflicts, there is something that is described as acceptable number of victims or collateral damage, et cetera. And tell me, what is the ratio between the killed soldiers and the killed civilians that does not constitute terrorising a population which is, if I may say so, an acceptable collateral damage? When does it reach certain point of ratio between the military and civilian victims when it is not acceptable?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you such a point. However, I -- you are simplifying my work, especially the work presented in the Karadzic Sarajevo report. I have done much more than just calculating the ratio and telling that the ratio is excessively high on more than 30 per cent of days. That was just the beginning of the analysis I completed. If I can take you to the report --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that later. We'll come to that. I'm only interested in the basics. You deduce that the civilian casualties among the residents of Sarajevo were the result of terror. I am asking you now to explain the criteria to us. And I also wanted to ask you about the methodology. Firstly, is the ratio the same in international conflicts and in civil wars? Is it the same in urban fighting or in fighting in open battle-fields? So if you propose some assertion, have you to explain to us how you arrived at that; and can you tell us which is this permissible line that has to be crossed in order for this to be considered terrorising?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you are right that if would be very useful to study this ratio in a number of conflicts. You are absolutely right. But this is a separate project which would be taking quite some resources as acquiring information, detailed information, and reliable information, about killings of civilians as part of armed conflict, is a challenge, I think. So what I did is much simpler than a study that would be broad in placing Sarajevo in a context of several other conflicts, and I explained the methodology in the report, and specifically so. So I can tell about what I did, and my conclusion related to terror is related to, first of all, causes of death of the killed civilians. There is a specific section in the report, Karadzic report and other Sarajevo reports, in which causes are expressed in terms of shelling and sniping, and other shooting. And a large per cent of killings was because of these causes. If there is no similarity and correspondence between killings of civilians and soldiers with time, and we know that soldiers are killed because of combat because they are part of the combat, so what would be -- what would be the reason for the killings of civilians is if causes of death are shelling, sniping, other shooting? So I think there is a very good reason that I said it was most likely a terror campaign, in which arms were involved that were killing civilians in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In other words, you are trying to say that the Serbs preferred to shoot at the civilians rather than at the Muslim soldiers.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I am not discussing the combat activities. I'm not discussing the army, the Serb army, the Bosniak army. I am telling what is the observation from the data used for Sarajevo killings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Doctor, yesterday or in last week, you stated that civilians were deliberately targeted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you remember having said that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What would that mean? So the soldiers intentionally tried to kill civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no information about the intentions. I can't say about the intentions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Because deliberate has some connotation in legal sense. How do you interpret that word, deliberate, deliberately targeting the civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The meaning for me, deliberate, was not related to combat activities. Causes of death being related to using arms against civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So would be differentiate "deliberate" with -- I will -- strike that. So how would that -- that meaning deliberate shelling or deliberate targeting differentiate with -- from, for example, reckless shelling, indiscriminate shelling, or disproportional shelling, in your opinion, as far as you can answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I would rather think of disproportionate shelling and sniping. Why? Because that they were shelled and killed by sniper is a fact. There are causes of death for the killed civilians that expressed the fact and because of the fact that there were many, many days on which the numbers of killed civilians were higher than soldiers. For me, in my assessment, it is disproportionate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, while we're on this subject, I want to take your mind back to a part of the cross-examination where Mr. Karadzic had put his case to you. Now what happened there, he -- he had squeezed in several questions in concertina fashion, you understand, and you weren't in a position to answer any of those questions. Now what I would like to do now is to dismantle that compound question and get your answers on each component of it, if possible. He said: First of all, my thesis is what happened there was a civil war. Are you in a position to answer yes or no to this question at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think I would rather not because I don't feel really familiar enough with legal aspect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Fair enough, all right. Thank you. He then said: "It was not that the Serbs persecuted others and nothing happened to the Serbs, and everything happened to others." Are you in a position to comment on that, one way or the other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as a layperson who reads about wars and conflicts, I know that every war is a complex situation, and there are more than just one party involved. So, also in the war in Bosnia, one party involved were the Serbs and the army and the paramilitaries but there were also other parties to conflict. And, again, I wouldn't like to go deeper than just that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you. And the last component of that compound suggestion was: "You will realise that everything was proportional there." Are you in a position to comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sure that not everything was proportionate in this war. I studied people killed in this war, both civilians and soldiers for the entire country of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I am sure that it is not that people lost their lives proportionally to ethnic composition pre-war ethnic composition or anything like that. Certain groups, I think, had lost more lives than other groups. But every -- every ethnic group, every people, every people suffered in this war, and considerably so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you very much, indeed, Doctor. Yes, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Excellency. I was waiting for the interpretation. Thank you for these clarifications. I am in a hurry, and therefore, I'm putting such questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] French language is a Baroque language and takes longer for interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So, in view of what His Excellency Baird asked you about, if I tell you that from your table among the displaced and the refugees, we have 32 percentages, or 34, it corresponds to the share in the overall population, and that equally applies to all three ethnic groups. This is the case with those who were killed as well. Approximately 32 percentage -- per cents of Serbs were among those who were killed, which is equal to their share, and my understand [as interpreted] of statistical analysis is to demonstrate these ratios.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: So -- so -- what -- what I need to say, for me, it is, if you want to calculate the shares, you can calculate the shares, but I don't think ... yeah, I don't know what to say. Sorry. You know ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Do you know that one party declared war on another party; that is to say, that the Muslims declared war on us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, it is not for the doctor to comment on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that there was the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Sarajevo, that they were blended among the population, and that it had the numbers which were three times larger than members of our army?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- I -- I don't know. I don't want to know perhaps even. I heard this theory before that Bosniak army was mixed up and was killing their own people, but I don't think I can comment on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, if, for example, we look the number of victims in 1994 from your report, starting from the 5th of February, and you noticed a large number of victims in that period, and I am sure that your coefficient definitely exceeded one. Just bear with me a minute. I need to find the year 1994 - I'm sure you have it in front of you - relating to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess you are referring to the Dragomir Milosevic report; right? Or Galic report? 1994, it is February. Galic report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Table number 13. You say that: "On the 5th of February, 1994, 45 civilians and 14 soldiers were killed, which totals 60, and the ratio is 1:4." Is that correct? Does this constitute terrorising civilians?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't have this ratio or this table calculated explicitly, but it might be that I have it somewhere in the text. This is a sample of days on which six or more civilians were killed. That is, Table 13, page 36, in the Galic report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know what happened on the 5th of February, 1994, in Sarajevo which resulted in this number of victims? Have you ever heard of Markale I incident?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know who caused it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's not for the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, if it is said that on the 8th of June, 1992, so-and-so number of civilians were killed in Sarajevo without taking into account that the Muslims launched their offensive on the 8th of June, 1992 -- look at this. It sayings eight civilians, 108 soldiers, total number is 116, and ratio 1:5. So if you take any date in which a considerable number of victims is recorded, then this requires to look into the matter who started this offensive, what was going on in the military terms, and whether this was merely a campaign of terror conducted by the Serbs. And, in addition to that, whether there was a siege or not in existence.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I note it is time to conclude your cross-examination, Mr. Karadzic. It is purely a waste of time to put such questions to Dr. Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Excellency, if the witness is taking the liberty to define what a siege is and what a terrorising campaign is, it is my right to say that this is incomplete data and that there is no proper contextualization. And I need to draw the attention of this witness that on those dates offensives were launched, that the 1st Corps of the BH Army had many more soldiers than we did, and they were more dangerous than our army. But, anyway, let's go back to the findings pertaining to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that during the war there existed part of the town which was called the Serbian Sarajevo and nowadays it is called eastern Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are referring to Pale, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No. I'm not talking about Pale. 80 per cent of the territory in Sarajevo was Serb controlled, and Serbs were a majority there. Do you know that there was a Serb majority in Ilijas, for example, but that we handed it over post-Dayton?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- I don't know what is the 80 per cent of the territory of Sarajevo that Serbs controlled territory and was it exactly. And Ilijas was indeed a Serb majority. But what's the question, actually?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The question is: Are you aware that throughout the whole war there existed two cities in Sarajevo, that the Serbian part of the town and Serbs territories by definition were located and were surrounding the Muslim part, and that did not mean that the town was under siege. That's why I'm asking you whether you know what Serb Sarajevo was.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly what you mean by "Serb Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, I need two more hours. Actually, I will try to finish until the end of today's working hours, but I would need more time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now please take a look at Sarajevo in the Karadzic case, and let us go together through the tables that you put.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sorry for the interruption. Just for the Trial Chamber's information, I do have some re-direct. My re-direct would be about five minutes long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Addendum A3. Table 1M.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: So that would be the municipalities report?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, Sarajevo Ten.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is P4994, e-court page 74.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we now please take a look at this page. I cannot give you the exact number. Yes. This is it. Could we now please take a look at this. There were over 43.000 adults in Sarajevo in 1991; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: 438.605 in Sarajevo Ten in 1991. All ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. How did you get this figure, that in the Serb part of Sarajevo there were only 24.000 when Serb Sarajevo included Trnovo, half of Ilidza, half of Hadzici, all of Vogosca, all of Ilijas, a small part of the old city and all of Pale?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This table is made for post-Dayton municipalities. So the part reported here as Republika Srpska includes parts out of a number of Sarajevo Ten municipalities that, after the Dayton Agreement, were assigned to Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Less look further on the sample of the population for 1997. What you indicate is that there was an increase in the Serb population to 29.000. Now what would you say if I were to tell you that now the population of Serb Sarajevo is 100.000?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is the Serb Sarajevo now? Is it the RS part?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Because we returned Hadzici, the Serb part of Hadzici. We returned the Serb part of Ilidza, almost all of Ilidza that is. Then we returned all of Vogosca and all of Ilijas, and that happened at the negotiating table in Dayton. What remained out of Sarajevo, Lukavica, and the rest, Pale and so on, that has a population of 100.000.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It might be. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Now take a look at this. You say that in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Sarajevo Ten in 1991, there were 205.000 Muslims and as for 1997, you give a lower figure. How did that happen?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a sample. It's a sample. Not a figure, complete figure. It's just a sample of Muslims identified in the voters' register which is 161.273.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we see Vogosca here? No, no.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have the next page now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Vogosca was in Serb hands throughout the war and that it was peacefully handed over after Dayton?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, I know that there was a Dayton Agreement in which the country was divided into Republika Srpska and the Federation of Bosniak and Croats. The analysis I made is using the post-Dayton municipalities. So I didn't study who had Vogosca before the war and after the war because it wasn't the subject of my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us take a look at 1C, the next table. Let us see how the Croats of Sarajevo faired. So let us take a look at this now. There were 31.000 Croats in Sarajevo in 1991. They accounted for 7.1 per cent. And let us see how things ended. 10.000 is the estimate, 4.4 per cent, or 37 per cent less; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: 10.000 is a sample. 1997 voters' register.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What does the sample show us? Does it not represent the whole?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is a sample of Croats registered in the 1997 voters' register. I don't think, Mr. Karadzic, that you will find in these numbers the answer to who was in charge of certain territories before the war and who became to be in charge after the war. Well, it is just a simple study of ethnic composition in 1991 and 1997, and no more than that. Things that happened during the war are not in this table, as a matter of fact, not explicitly reported as numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And conclusions cannot be made in a criminal case; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's not for the witness, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Then nothing -- can we have 1S. Can we just cast a glance and see how the Serbs faired? And then we'll move on to something different.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this correct, that in Sarajevo in 1991, there were 133.000 Serbs who were adults; namely, born before 1980.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And if I were to tell you that in Sarajevo at the time there were 157.000 Serbs, persons who declared themselves that way, and 23.000 who declared themselves as Yugoslav, and that included an enormous number of Serbs, does that correspond to the number that you have there of persons born before 1980?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't. But I would like to hear about your sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The official census in Sarajevo. There were 157.000 Serbs; a bit more than that. And there were 23.000-something Yugoslavs. All of them, not only those who were of age.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is correct. I have the published number of Serbs in Sarajevo, all ten municipalities, all ages, and this is 157.000 Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So let us please take a look at this. In the area that belonged to Republika Srpska, you believed that there are persons who were born before 1980 and that there 18.000-something of them and in the federal part, 115.000; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the estimate is, or, what, that in 1997, there's 82 per cent less Serbs, Serbs in relation to Serbs. That would be 91 per cent less, according to my calculations, in the federal part and 55.4 per cent more in the Serb part of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have 82.2 per cent less Serbs in the federal part of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But my calculation is 91 in relation to the 115.000. That is the number of people who were there in 1991. But, all right. This cannot be used because we don't know what a sample is and what the population it represents is. At any rate, the estimate is that in 1997 there are only 5 per cent Serbs in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the federal part of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, in the federal part of Sarajevo. And there were 30 per cent of them; right? There used to be 30 per cent?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: 28. So about. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we take a look at 2S? Table 2S.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: E-court 88.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you help me with this. This minimum number of internally displaced persons from Sarajevo Ten, the Serb's status as of 1997; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And, in 1997, isn't that right, 76.100 Serbs, 11.000 of which are Republika Srpska, and 64.000 in the Federation of BH. That is to say, displaced persons and refugees; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see 1D05559 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you recognise this table?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You -- not you, but Mr. Robinson asked me to provide statistics, if I had them, on deaths and disappearances of Muslims from a number of municipalities in 1992-1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So in Bratunac, there were 21.535 Muslims; right? And there are 3.281 killed or disappeared, which is 15.2 per cent.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is what is -- it is in the table.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please let's go through the whole table so that I don't have to read all of it. Foca, 20.790. Kljuc, 17.696 Muslims, 600 Muslims killed and disappeared, 3.4 per cent. Prijedor, 49.351 inhabitants, 2.627 killed and disappeared, 3.5 per cent. Sanski Most, 28.136, 619 killed and disappeared, 2.2 per cent. Vlasenica, 18.727, 1.197 Muslims killed and disappeared, 6.4 per cent. Zvornik, 48.102, 3.411 Muslims killed and disappeared, 2.7 -- 7.1 per cent. For all of Bosnia and Herzegovina there were 1.902.956 Muslims. 49.111 Muslims killed and disappeared, 2.6 per cent. Did these figures include combatants who were killed in fighting?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does it include persons who died a natural death?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, natural deaths.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does the Bratunac figure include the number of persons who lost their lives in 1995?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the complete war period. Until end of war in 1995, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would it be correct to conclude that throughout the war less than 3 per cent of the Muslim population lost their lives, 2.6 per cent?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what the table says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you happen to know what the percentage would be of Jews who lost their lives in Europe during the Holocaust in the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Not relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Actually, Mr. President, if I could just be heard on that. I think it is relevant. Maybe she knows or she doesn't. But these are the seven municipalities that the Prosecution has alleged in the indictment, paragraph 38, which constituted genocide as charged in count 1 of the indictment and one of the elements of genocide is that there has to be an intend to destroy a substantial part of the group. You see here that 2.6 per cent were "destroyed," and I think it's relevant to compare that with other instances where there have been findings of genocide such as the Holocaust or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Pardon, Mr. Robinson. I'm sorry to cut you off, but is this for this witness to confirm?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, he's asking her for a piece of information. If she has it then it would be useful to the Chamber, if she doesn't then we will have to find it through some other source.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we can safely skip this issue with this witness. Mr. Karadzic, please conclude your cross-examination in five minutes' time from now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say, then, to Dr. Tabeau what my case is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If necessary.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In Rwanda, Dr. Tabeau, about 70 per cent of the Tutsi population was destroyed, and in Europe about 58 per cent of the population that were Jews --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau didn't deal with the legal motion of genocide deportation or anything else.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this table be admitted? Quite simply, so that it would be an instrument, a tool, so that you could see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2250, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Tabeau. And my apologies. I was just after the facts. I appreciate your work and I appreciate your testimony.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, earlier today you had a few questions from the President and Judge Baird and they regarded the parts of your report in which -- part of your Sarajevo report in which you spoke about timing, and you spoke about the timing of deaths of civilians versus the timing of deaths versus soldiers [sic]. Do you remember that discussion?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And at one point, you were specifically asked how the meaning deliberate shelling or deliberate targeting differentiate with, for example, from reckless shelling, indiscriminate shelling or disproportional shelling. And you were asked whether you could give an answer to that. And answer you said would -- you rather thought would be disproportionate shelling and sniping, and then you went on to say: "There are causes of death that for the killed civilians that expressed the fact and because of that fact there were many, many days on which the numbers of killed civilians were higher than soldiers. For me, in my assessment, it is disproportionate." When you were using the term "disproportionate," were you using that term as a statistical definition, one that regarded numbers, or were you using it in a legal sense?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was using it in a statistical sense. I cannot use a legal term because I am not a lawyer. I didn't go to the law school.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And did your study on this particular issue of timing speak to any legal determinations as to cause of death or were you only doing a comparison between numbers, between civilian deaths versus soldiers' death?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are comparing civilian deaths with soldiers' deaths and causes of death are studied in these context.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, I also want to speak to you about something that has been brought up yesterday and today and it is the reliability of the OSCE records as a source in matching. This was brought up yesterday at transcript 28304, 28305, and then today. The President very precisely put the question about whether you were saying that 1997 census was not 100 percent reliable, and I would like to discuss that issue now. In a perfect statistical or demographic world, what two sources or what source would you deem to be the most reliable to be used as bookends in a matching exercise?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mentioned this during my testimony, that ideally I would like to work with two censuses, one at the outbreak of the conflict and another thereafter.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And can you tell us the reasons for that, why a census is a very good source?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are many, many reasons for this, I think. It is the methodology of census and the coverage of census and the way of reporting of data in the census that make it so special and so reliable.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, if another source, if you found another source that adopted the census data or, say, copied the census data, would you consider that second source to also be reliable?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. If it would be copied, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So let's look at the OSCE voters' registration and the information upon it was based. First tell us this: What was the pre-condition with which perspective voters had to comply in order to be eligible to vote?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: They have to be at age 18 or older and they had to be listed on the census, of course. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And when that person came in to register to vote how was it checked that they were on the census?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, a copy of the census records, a portion of the census, personal items, including JMBG and names and the date of birth and municipality of residence in 1991, there was a copy of the census in every registration office and actually there were hard copies. That means, I don't know, volumes, ten volumes or so, books with the census information. There also was an electronic version of the census available as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 17956, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
