utterances.text: Can I intervene briefly, Ms. West. Going back to the 1997 voters' register, talking about 2.5 million, you just stated that they had to be listed on the census already.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you remember my previous question, where the .7 million go? We discussed 1.8 million.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And your answer was they should be matched with --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, with the census. Yeah, match with the census, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But 2.5 million are already listed on the census. That means they should have been matched.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think more are listed in the census. More are listed in the census. Actually, all eligible voters available from 1991 should be listed on the census, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We talk about 2.5 million --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Million. Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- in voters' register.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In order to register, they already should already -- they should appear --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the census, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- on the 1991 census. So 2.5 million are those who already were matched with the census, were they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not electronically. You know, in principle, as a matter of principle, yes. All should have been matched but matching this quantities of information is a challenging activity. There are many little things that prevent 100 per cent matching rate. And these are, you know, like, differences in formats of items like JMBG could have been formatted slightly differently. Commas could have been inserted or spaces, and names perhaps could have been presented differently. So it is a huge mass of material that were processed by different people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And following up on Mr. President's question, so in theory the match you did was the second match between the OSCE records and the census; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I guess the OSCE was the first ones to match because they had to prepare the register, which was used for the registration of individuals. Yes, absolutely. OSCE were the first ones to -- to work with this material. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So here in front of us we see a letter dated November 2008. Are you familiar with this letter?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, yes. That is a letter from OSCE to the Prosecutor of ICTY in which actually he confirms the fact that the OSCE was using the census data for the register, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And here it says: "After meticulous review of our records we can confirm that the 1991 census for BiH was used as the sole basis for the registration of eligible voters in the 1997 ... elections. Besides, the same records reveal that both electronic and paper versions of the 1991 census ... were made available to each and every registration centre throughout the entire 1997 voters registration exercise." Did OTP receive this letter as a result of your inquiry?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yep.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So, from your understanding, did the OSCE registration process include adopting or copying over the census information onto the registration for those who wanted to vote?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I guess so, yes. They were working with the census material.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And knowing that, what is your opinion as to the reliability of the information in the voters' registration regarding name, date of birth, and JMBG number?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is very good. As I said earlier today, it is a very reliable source to be used in this kind of analysis as I used it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: In the absence of a census-to-census matching exercise, what is your opinion as to the statistical reliability of the 1991 census match to the OSCE voters' registration?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is very reliable way of doing things.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one brief question, please, Excellencies. I'll tell you what it is. What happened to those who did not register, who didn't wish to vote? Where are they? Are they considered to be missing, disappeared, because registering to vote is a voluntarily matter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think that is clear from the previous answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But can I confirm that they are just not in the register. That only means that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unless my colleagues have questions for you. Oh, yes, I have one matter. I am raising this, Ms. West, because I already noted the Defence letter to the OSCE. Dr. Tabeau during the course of your evidence you stated that the -- all the source material must have been disclose to the Defence but as regards 1996 voters' register, I don't know the exact name, but 1996 election material was not disclosed to the Defence because it was not the practice of the Tribunal, since it was not used in your report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't use it, and I even don't have a copy of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You don't have a copy of it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If a copy is needed, then Karadzic has to address this request to the OSCE, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, my question was -- I'm sorry, I was overlapping. My question was whether have you in your possession that material but it is clear it doesn't -- you do not have it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And the Prosecution does not have it either.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I will double-check, but I'm fairly certain we do not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Then that concludes your evidence, Dr. Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: On behalf of my colleagues I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just one -- after one matter, we'll rise all together.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, we are seized of your motion to temporarily stay the application of the Chamber's decision on ICMP exhibits and we also received the Defence response. To me, it's not clear what you are seeking. Are you seeking the stay in relation to all the exhibits or only in relation to those which are to be reclassified fully, that is, without any redaction? Oh, yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We are seeking an extension of time for those exhibits that we listed in our response. Included in those exhibits are some of the very large ones which is why we have asked for the 18th which would include the ICMP database --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So, i.e., you are seeking only an extension of time for Exhibit P4639, 4640, and P4641.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I don't have it in front of me, but I don't believe so. I think more than that are listed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You listed about nine or -- or 11. So you -- you are seeking a stay with respect to all = the documents therein.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So my question was whether you had different Rule 70 conditions or ...

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: In addition to that, we're seeking a stay, we're also seeking a stay as regards discussions with ICMP and any potential Rule 70 conditions. I can tell you that we are in the process of having those discussions and there is an expectation we will be filing something else as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any observation on the Defence's response?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I did see the Defence response, and it regarded those discussions with ICMP. I can report to the Court at this point that the second response is being drafted as we speak, and it will be a motion for reconsideration based on those discussions. But in the meanwhile, since the due date is today and the material is so voluminous, that is why we filed the separate motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Hearing is now adjourned for today, and we resume tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
